When I’m dropping the pin for where I saw a bird there is a map, and I can move around and see my other pins. Where is that map? Possibly the world's best field guide. Want to identify a bird that you got just a glimpse of? With a print field guide, even a good one, that could take a while as you sort through possibly hundreds of pictures and descriptions trying to figure out just what you saw. On the other hand, Merlin puts together your location and your description of the bird to automatically create a list of the most probable species. No detective work needed. The audio ID feature is one I don't use often (I've also yet to try the picture one), but what I've seen so far is good.
 Oh, and the app covers every bird in existence and some birds not in existence! You can find out about birds you've never heard of (Subdesert Mesite), laugh at dumb names (Lizard Buzzard), and even find examples of recently extinct birds (including the overabundance of extinct Hawaiian honeycreepers) by downloading bird packs or using the search feature. You can also see the former range of the Carolina Parakeet (R.I.P.), hear what a Happy Wren sounds like, and wonder who on earth named the "Naked-faced Spiderhunter."
 There are just two problems with this otherwise great app. One is that "most probable bird" doesn't mean "every possible bird." Occasionally you will see that unambiguous Summer Tanager where you "shouldn't." In that case, it won't register as a possible bird, and your sighting can't be saved. Second, your sightings are difficult to delete from your life list, so a misidentification can haunt you forever. (Whoops.)
 Other than those, the only real problems are with performance, not function. This app used to freeze and crash a lot on me, but that issue seems to have been fixed (for now, at least). The only other concern I've come across is that some bird profiles always those for extinct ones consistently throw up a "you're offline" message, even with good connection. Still, I don't know if they're truly not loading or are just placeholders.

Unethical Features According to Cornell Staff. The app is great and works very well, unfortunately, it doesn't currently follow the guidelines for ethical wildlife photography according to the Audubon Society and several Cornell professors. Please consider removing the onboard phone camera id function. It requires people to get too close to id the subject and could cause harm to the animal or its environment. Flash is enabled by default in the ios app. This is also considered to be unethical and potentially harmful. "flash blindness": The photoreceptor cells might sustain temporary damage and would not "dark adapt" to the same level of sensitivity. This could lessen the bird's visual acuity at night, and it could take longer to recover from being flashed. That would be particularly problematic if the bird is flashed when flying, as it might collide with an obstacle while temporarily blinded, or when adults are feeding their young and need to be searching for prey. "It takes a while to readjust after being flashed in the dark, and if during that time, a bird had to perform some critical life function, it would be at a disadvantage," Loew says. "During that period, it could not effectively hunt." - Ellis Loew, professor of physiology at Cornell University Some quotes from Audubon.org "Avoid causing unnecessary disturbance or stress to birds."
"Use a telephoto lens and maintain enough distance to allow your subject to behave naturally." "If you're using a macro lens [or] a wide-angle lens, even if you're operating the camera remotely, you're probably too close.
Telephoto lenses of at least 500mm are recommended."

Great… could be better. As someone who spends way too much time staring into trees trying to decide if that tiny blur is a warbler or just a leaf, I really do enjoy the Merlin app from Cornell Lab of Ornithology. The best part is that you do not need expensive microphones, binoculars, or fancy birding gear to use it. You can just pull out your phone, hit sound ID, and suddenly Merlin is telling you there are six birds screaming at each other in the woods that you never would have noticed.

That said, I wish Merlin worked a little more like iNaturalist. Right now, it feels like Merlin identifies bird sounds and then they disappear into the void. I would love to see it isolate the actual bird call, upload it into a shared database, and let other users listen and confirm whether the identification is correct. Sometimes Merlin tells me there is a rare bird nearby and I need a second opinion before I sprint into the woods looking like a lunatic.

I also think Cornell should work more closely with iNaturalist so birders, hunters, wildlife students, and all the other birders out there can contribute to larger animal tracking and population studies. There is a lot of value in everyday people recording what they hear and see. Plus, it would make birding feel even more like a team sport.

Overall, Merlin is an awesome app and one of the easiest ways to get into birding. I just think it could become even better if it leaned harder into community science and let users help verify what the app hears.

The best set of extra ears. I have been using versions of Merlin for four years now, and it has consistently gotten better over time. When used properly, it’s like having a friend who has “ear birded” for decades along with you, catching things that may (if you’re like me) be outside your hearing range because of tinnitus or other hearing loss. But you have to be aware of the limitations of AI sound recognition and not use Merlin as your only way of tallying the birds around you. 
Merlin can occasionally “hallucinate” a bird recognition because of collisions of other noises that have sound prints similar to the bird in question. Camera shutter noises can be mistaken by the software for a Great Blue Heron, for example, or a squeaking piece of gear for a Killdeer. Being aware of which birds are likely to be where you are and paying attention to the probability score that comes up for each bird detected are important in using Merlin for ID in the field. If a bird is rare where you are, and it only pops up on Merlin once, and you didn’t hear it yourself, it probably isn’t there and you should not put that ID on eBird. Always use the detection as a prompt to look for the bird or listen for it yourself, not as a reason for a sighting all by itself. 
Stability of the app has improved greatly, but it still depends on microphone access not being interrupted by other apps. Cellular signal strength may affect whether you can save a session. It is best to use the app for periods of no more than 10 minutes at a time to make sure you can save sessions quickly and reliably in my experience. 
This app is free, but if you use it frequently you should definitely donate to Cornell’s Lab of Ornithology to support the technical and scientific work behind it and eBird.

Genuinely a Life-changing App, a Detailed Review. I absolutely love Merlin. It really made me confident about identifying, confirming, and memorizing birds and their many mesmerizing songs. Its features are convenient and easy to use, while also being massively helpful. The capture range for birdsong is great and impressive at times on just an iPhone with no specialized equipment, and is incredibly accurate. Personally, over 4+ months of use, I have never encountered an inaccuracy. They also have an amazing function where you can import audio containing birdsong, and it will analyze and identify it, also personally proven correct in every usage. 

Every serious birder I’ve known or met, friend or not, uses Merlin and trusts them as do I. I have nothing but good experiences with them.

Check out their website(s) too! They list bird-related events all over the US (and maybe elsewhere? I’m sure their site has multiple versions curated over the countries, but don’t take that as fact) and provide many other services such as detailed info on migrations in their Migration Dashboard. They certainly have their heart and soul in this and really care about birds and birding, contributing priceless data and tools to the masses for no cost, hassle, or struggle. For a name that admittedly has the monopoly over birding sites, they prove why they do very easily. Support them and their amazing quality!

My only suggestions, not gripes, are:

I would like to be able to multi-use the app. When I want to listen to the calls of a certain bird in-app, I have to stop my recording. Being able to listen to the calls I want from the bird i’ve selected/searched while still keeping my recording going would be great, and would help me identify birds Merlin can’t pick up from far away on just an iPhone while keeping it going to capture any calls it can, enabling full utilization.

More data! For the beginning birder, memorizing the names of all the birds even in their local area can possibly prove difficult. Many names or moreso nicknames change across regions, and different people may know the birds as different things. If it were possible to input a local dub for the bird, such as inputting a regional nickname of the American Woodcock: the ‘Timberdoodle’ in the search and it resulting with the Woodcock, it would make the app more accessible and fun to use for especially beginners, bringing more much-needed individuals into the hobby.
